opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to be honest that automation work creates a particular kind of tension. If you're building systems that might change or replace parts of people's jobs, including your own colleagues' jobs, people can feel they have a stake in not saying certain things. They might worry that raising a concern sounds like special pleading, or that pointing out a failure mode makes them look like they're slowing things down. So you have to work against that deliberately rather than assume openness will just happen.

One thing I've found useful is separating the question of "is this a good idea" from "who proposed it." If disagreement is about the object-level claim, about evidence and arguments, then people can push back on a senior person's plan without it feeling like a personal challenge. That sounds obvious, but it takes repeated modeling from the people with authority. If a leader visibly changes their mind in a meeting because someone junior made a good point, and says so, that does more than any written policy.

A second piece is making uncertainty normal to express. A lot of the important things in safety and in automation generally are things where nobody really knows the answer. If the culture rewards confident statements, people who have a nagging worry they can't fully articulate will just stay quiet, and those half-formed worries are often exactly what you need to hear early. So I like norms where it's fine to say "I'm maybe 20% on this, but here's something that bothers me," and that gets taken seriously rather than dismissed because it isn't a finished argument.

Third, you want multiple channels. Some people are comfortable arguing in a big meeting; many aren't. Written docs where people can comment asynchronously, small one-on-ones, and, for the really sensitive stuff, ways to raise concerns that don't route through your direct manager. That last one matters especially if the concern is about the direction of the organization itself, about whether something should be deployed at all. People need to know there's a path for that which won't cost them.

And finally, I'd say you have to actually act on what you hear, or at least explain clearly why you didn't. Nothing kills a speaking-up culture faster than people raising things and seeing them disappear into a void. If someone flags a risk and you decide to proceed anyway, close the loop: here's what we considered, here's why we weighed it this way, and here's what would change our minds. That keeps people engaged and makes it worth their while to keep telling you uncomfortable things.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more important questions, and it's one where I've changed my mind somewhat over time. The naive version of the answer is "just tell people it's fine to speak up," and that basically doesn't work. People are extremely good at reading what's actually rewarded versus what's nominally rewarded, and if the nominal message is "raise concerns" but the actual pattern is that people who raise concerns get sidelined or slow things down and then nobody thanks them, people will stop within a few months.

So I'd break it into a few pieces. The first is that the leadership has to actually want the information, in the sense that it changes decisions. If someone raises a safety concern or a "this automation is going to break in this edge case" concern, and the decision visibly moves as a result, that is worth more than any number of all-hands speeches about psychological safety. And the inverse is true too: if the decision never moves, people correctly infer that speaking was pointless.

The second piece is that you want to lower the cost of being wrong. A lot of why people don't speak is not fear of retaliation exactly, it's fear of looking foolish, or of having wasted everyone's time. So you want a culture where raising a concern that turns out to be a non-issue is treated as a cheap, normal event. In my experience the places that do this well have a lot of low-stakes channels: written docs with comment threads, a norm of flagging something with "probably nothing, but" and that being a completely acceptable move. Written culture helps a lot here, actually, because it's less socially expensive to leave a comment than to interrupt a meeting, and it leaves a record so the concern can't just evaporate.

The third piece, which is specific to automation and to AI in particular, is that you need to separate the question "is this concern technically correct" from "is this person being an obstacle." When you're automating things, there's a built-in tension: the whole point is to move faster and remove humans from loops, and the person saying "wait" is structurally in the way. So you have to design around that. One thing that helps is having people whose explicit job it is to find problems, so that the concern comes from a role rather than from an individual who's sticking their neck out. Another is to make the people doing the automation also responsible for the failure modes, so that raising a concern isn't someone else's team slowing you down, it's your own team catching your own bug.

And then the last thing I'd say is that leaders have to model it, and specifically model being wrong in public. If the most senior people never say "I was wrong about that" or "I missed this, thanks for catching it," then everyone below them learns that admitting error is something you do when you're junior. Whereas if the senior people do it routinely, it becomes just how the organization talks. That's a cheap intervention that I think is underused, partly because it's uncomfortable.

I'd also add, honestly, that none of this is a substitute for having external accountability. Internal culture can get you a long way, but there are limits to how much any organization can be relied on to surface its own problems, especially when there's commercial pressure. So I'd want the communication culture to be good, and I'd also want there to be routes outside the organization, whether that's regulators, external researchers, or just norms about what gets published. Those two things reinforce each other rather than being alternatives.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to make it possible to say, “I don’t think this is working,” without that being interpreted as, “I’m not committed to the mission.” If you’re pursuing automation, you need people to be able to distinguish enthusiasm for the goal from confidence in a particular approach.

And that depends much more on what happens when someone raises a concern than on what you say about your culture. Does the concern get investigated? Does the person get credit for finding a problem? Are senior people willing to say, “Yes, that changes my mind”? People watch those interactions and learn whether speaking up is actually useful.

There’s also a particular tension with automation: you’re asking people to help build something that may change or eliminate their own role. You should be candid about that uncertainty. If people think expressing a concern will threaten their position, or that leadership has already decided what the answer must be, you’re going to lose information you need.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to make it possible to say, “I don’t think this is working,” even when that’s inconvenient for the organization. If you’re pursuing automation, you’re asking people to help build systems that may change their own jobs, so there’s an obvious tension there. You shouldn’t expect people to feel comfortable just because you’ve told them to speak up.

A lot depends on what happens when someone actually raises a concern. Does the person leading the project get defensive? Does the concern get a serious response? Can someone admit that they don’t know whether a system is safe or reliable without that being treated as a failure? Those reactions establish the culture much more than a statement of values does.

I’d want leaders to be explicit about uncertainty themselves, and to make room for disagreement before decisions become commitments that everyone feels obliged to defend. You can have confidential channels as well, but ideally people should also see ordinary, public examples of someone challenging a plan and being listened to. That makes the invitation to speak credible.
